newsitem.title: USA: 1996 campaign fuzzy on all but negative issues.
newsitem.headline: 1996 campaign fuzzy on all but negative issues.

text.p: The 1996 U.S. presidential race seemed to lack a great stirring issue -- or any issue at all until campaign financing gave Bob Dole and Ross Perot an opening to bash President Bill Clinton in the waning days.

That may provide a handy summary of what by any measure has been a listless contest: lacking the grand themes that have stirred some past campaigns -- economic discontent, Cold War tensions, social upheavals -- the rivals seized on low ones of ethics and character questions.

"It's been a relatively issueless, passionless campaign. It's hard for me to remember one that was as issueless and passionless as this one," said Stephen Hess, a senior fellow in governmental studies at the Brookings Institution.

The possible exception was the campaign finance issue that boiled up a few weeks before the November 5 ballot and gave Republican Dole and Reform Party nominee Perot a chance to question Clinton's ethics and character in a way that finally seemed to do him some damage.

Their attacks were fuelled by a stream of news reports about the activities of one John Huang, a Democratic Party fundraiser and former Commerce Department official under Clinton who collected large sums of questionable political campaign cash from Asian contacts.

The implication raised by critics -- and rejected by Clinton's spokesmen -- was that he or his strategists may have peddled access to U.S. trade or foreign policymakers, or at least given foreigners improper influence in U.S. politics.

Some late opinion polls showed a tightening in the race with Dole whittling down Clinton's double-digit leads and undecided voters breaking his way. The assumption was that the trend was driven in part by the ethics attacks.

After trying to ignore the issue, Clinton addressed it in a speech only on Friday, blaming the Republicans for the lack of effective campaign finance laws and proposing reforms of his own. They included bans on donations from foreign-owned U.S. businesses and from individuals who are not citizens.
That was about as close to a hot international issue as Clinton-Dole campaigns ever came -- and their sharpest clash on anything that might be called a distinguishing issue.

Among the reasons for that was the fact that Clinton and Dole are not ideological opposites, and they obscured what substantive differences they do have by positioning themselves smack in the middle of the political spectrum.
For example, Clinton upset some liberal Democrats by signing a welfare reform bill, while Dole shunned the calls of Republican right-wingers for a constitutional amendment banning abortion.

Clinton co-opted some issues Republicans thought were theirs, like crime and family values. He blurred the distinctions on others like affirmative-action programmes to promote equal opportunity in employment and education.
Perhaps most important, with the United States in an economic expansion and at peace, the economy and foreign policy were but small blips on the campaign radar screen.
"Dole has searched and searched for one issue with which he could beat Clinton. He's never been able to find one," said Mark Rozell, a political scientist at American University.

Early in the year, tax reform promised to be a hot-button issue as publishing magnate Steve Forbes campaigned for a flat income tax rate in the Republican primaries. Trade figured prominently too, with conservative commentator Pat Buchanan blasting Clinton for giving "trade favours" to China.

Dole defeated Buchanan and Forbes to win the Republican nomination but embraced some of their causes. Although Dole had been a free-trader, he accused Clinton of selling out workers with his trade policy. He had been a fiscal conservative, but proposed a 15 percent tax cut.
But public interest in the trade issue receded and Americans apparently found the tax cut pledge hard to believe.
Dole did try to attack Clinton on the economy, arguing that economic growth didn't compare so well with past expansions. That didn't take America by storm either.

"The fact is that Clinton is the first president who has not had a recession in the first term in 25 years. No matter how much Republicans complain about the rate of economic growth, people are better off now than four years ago," said Republican strategist William Kristol.

One issue that lingered quietly on some voters' minds was the perception that, at 73, Dole was too old to be president. The 50-year-old Clinton dealt with this gingerly but pointedly by calling his own leadership as a "bridge to the future."
